chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
title: Union 802 required quitting the band; the Army Service Force band
summary: Crawford says 802 would admit them only if they quit the band, then describes two years playing marches at Camp Kilmer.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: What were the requirements for getting in the union in those days?

Well, I don't know what the joining fee was, I've forgotten. But the requirement -- we were union men, but we were unionized in Buffalo, New York. 533, that was the number of that local in Buffalo. But to get in 802, which is the New York musician's union, well, you just had to either quit the band -- that's it, quit the band and join the union. They wouldn't let us in that union unless we had quit the band. I had to quit, because when Uncle Sam reached out for World War II, I went in the army to play drums, not to carry a gun and to go over and shoot and kill.

So I played two years in the Army Service force band at Camp Kilmer, right over here in Jersey. Yes, that's all I did, played drums. Military drums, man, I can see right now. I'm practicing marches, such as Semper Fidelis, and various marches. You had to play the troops over on the boats, of course, we did, we played them right to the gangplank, and turned around and went back to camp. And then we met them as they came back from the war and play them off the boats. That was my duty. Playing with this large Army Service force band.

And so, I don't know what happened to most of the fellows. Joe Turner, piano player, he played bass (inaudible) in the band, and people like that. He's in Europe somewhere, Belgium or somewhere. The other guys was scattered about, some

of them gone, some of them died, but the remainder, I didn't keep in touch with them, much. Not that I didn't want to, but I was just in my thing. I had to go make a living and a name for Jimmy Crawford. And that's what I did to the best of my ability. I went through hell, man, I went -- and I know I know a lot, and I have a lot of experiences that I witnessed. My memoirs are treasurable. I just -- I'm proud of knowing what I know about travelling from Maine to Florida, New York to California, and halfway around the world, Scandinavia, India, Great Britain, France. I didn't play in Italy, but I went through there just to find out what was happening.

Wonderful. Only thing, I wasn't involved or interested in women, as most bandsmen do. All I wanted to do was to hear music, and I got some bands in my mind, Speed Webb, which I first heard Roy Eldridge. I don't know where Speed was from, I think around -- well, anyway, out in the Middle West or somewhere, Indiana or somewhere. McKinney's Kenny's Cotton Pickers, Zack White, Helvey's band. Oh, they were the swingingest bands in the land. Alphonso Alphonso Trent --
